title: Checkpoint: Life in a Medieval Town
objective: After this level you can describe work, trade, food and fun in a medieval town.
summary: Medieval towns created a new kind of person, the walled-town dweller or bourgeois. A timeline from the revival after 1000 to 1405 ties the chapter together.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: the medieval town invented a new kind of person.
cards.body: Not a lord, not a peasant, but someone who lived behind a town wall. Medieval France had a word for them, and you still use it.

events.label: Henry V’s charters: city air brings freedom
The Champagne fairs at their peak
England’s law on who may wear what
Christine de Pizan’s City of Ladies

cards.headline: The first bourgeois
cards.body: In medieval France, a bourgeois was someone who lived in a walled town, as distinct from a peasant. Picture the townspeople of this chapter: burgesses tempted by a rival windmill, brewsters selling ale, guild craftsmen climbing from apprentice to master, merchants at the weekly market. Their towns ran on charters from bishops, counts and kings. Today the bourgeoisie means the social order dominated by the middle class. The walled town handed the modern world a word.

mascot.line: Markets, guilds, mills, feasts and football: you just walked the whole town. Nicely done.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: Towns revived after 1000 and charters promised freedom
Markets, fairs and guilds organised trade and work
Mills, food and clothes all marked who had power
Women worked, wrote and ran estates, within legal limits
The walled-town dweller gave us the word bourgeois

questions.prompt: In the story of medieval towns, which order of events is right?

options.label: Windmills in English records, the 1363 apparel law, the City of Ladies
The 1363 apparel law, windmills in English records, the City of Ladies
The City of Ladies, the 1363 apparel law, windmills in English records
options.rationale: The City of Ladies came last, in 1405.

options.label: Windmills in English records, the City of Ladies, the 1363 apparel law

questions.prompt: At a medieval English fair or market, what was a piepowder court for?

options.label: Licensing new weekly markets
Settling traders’ disputes on the spot
Testing the quality of flour
options.rationale: That was about mills and guilds.

options.label: Punishing people who wore the wrong cloth
options.rationale: That was the job of sumptuary law.

questions.explanation: Piepowder (“dusty feet”) courts settled disputes at fairs and markets quickly and on the spot.

questions.prompt: The word “bourgeois” began in medieval France. What did it first mean?

options.label: A knight who owned a castle
options.rationale: That’s a lord, not a town dweller.

options.label: A peasant who farmed a lord’s land
options.rationale: The word set town dwellers apart from peasants.

options.label: Someone who lived in a walled town
A monk who copied books

questions.explanation: A bourgeois was an inhabitant of a walled town, as distinct from a peasant; the word later named the middle class.

questions.prompt: What did Abbot Samson fear would happen if Herbert the dean’s windmill stayed up?

options.label: It would block the view of the abbey
It would catch fire and burn the town
The king would tax the abbey more
The burgesses would grind their grain there instead of at his mills

questions.explanation: Samson said the burgesses would take their grain to the dean’s mill, costing his own mills their toll.

questions.prompt: Level 54’s lower-ranking diners drank plenty of ale. Who brewed and sold most of the ale in medieval England?

options.label: Women
Monks alone
options.rationale: Most ale was brewed and sold by women.

options.label: The king’s household
Merchants at the Champagne fairs
options.rationale: The fairs traded cloth and spices.

questions.explanation: Women brewed and sold most of the ale consumed in medieval England; after 1350, men slowly took over.
